title: Date and time functions from time.h
learningObjectives: Explain the roles of time_t and struct tm, and distinguish ISO C calendar-time facilities from platform-specific high-resolution or monotonic clock APIs.
Obtain calendar time with time(), check its failure sentinel, and distinguish a timestamp from a human-readable date.
Convert a time value to broken-down local or UTC time using localtime() and gmtime(), including their shared static-storage caveat.
Format calendar fields with strftime() and interpret its return value as the number of characters written, excluding the terminating null character.
Compare elapsed time with difftime() and distinguish elapsed-time measurement from calendar scheduling and monotonic timing.
Write portable, defensive date/time code that checks library results, avoids retaining pointers to overwritten static results, and documents timezone assumptions.
prerequisites: CL1.3 C program structure and syntax
CL2.4 Fundamental data types and object sizes

understand.concept: The C standard library groups calendar-time facilities in <time.h>. A time value such as time_t represents a calendar-time quantity defined by the implementation; it is not safe to assume a universal integer width, epoch, timezone, or textual format. A broken-down calendar value uses struct tm fields such as tm_year (years since 1900), tm_mon (0–11), tm_mday (1–31), tm_hour, tm_min and tm_sec. Formatting turns these fields into text; it does not change the underlying time.
understand.whyItMatters: Programs use dates for logs, reports, file names, event records and user-facing timestamps. Confusing UTC with local time, assuming time_t is always a 64-bit integer, or ignoring conversion failures can create incorrect records and portability defects.
understand.analogy: A timestamp is like a point on a timeline; a broken-down calendar structure is like the year/month/day/hour labels shown on a wall calendar.
understand.analogyLimit: Calendar labels depend on timezone and calendar rules. A time_t representation and its range are implementation-defined, and wall-clock time can change; the analogy does not make it a monotonic stopwatch.

explain.narrative:
<time.h> separates several jobs. time(&value) obtains the current calendar time and returns (time_t)-1 on failure. localtime(&value) and gmtime(&value) convert a time value into a struct tm, commonly through library-managed static storage; copy the structure immediately if it must be retained. strftime() writes a formatted representation into a caller-owned character array and returns zero when the result does not fit. difftime(later, earlier) returns the difference in seconds as a double and avoids assuming that subtracting two time_t values is portable.

The standard C calendar-time interface is not a general high-resolution or monotonic timer. For elapsed performance measurements, use a platform facility designed for monotonic clocks and document that dependency. Timezone databases, daylight-saving rules and locale-sensitive formatting are environment concerns; do not hard-code assumptions about them.

examples.title: Format a known calendar value without depending on the machine clock
examples.explanation: The structure is initialized to zero before selected fields are assigned. tm_year is measured from 1900 and tm_mon is zero-based. strftime writes into the caller's buffer; its nonzero return confirms that formatted output was produced.

examples.title: Compare two time values with difftime
examples.explanation: This example uses two representable time_t values and asks difftime for their difference. It does not assume that time_t is a signed integer that can safely be subtracted directly.

practise.guidedTask: Change the sample calendar fields to represent a different date. Predict tm_year and tm_mon before running, then verify the formatted string. Next, shorten the output buffer and observe how the program handles strftime returning zero.
practise.independentTask: Write a small timestamp formatter that calls time(), checks for (time_t)-1, converts to local calendar time, copies the returned struct tm immediately, and checks the result of strftime before printing.
hints: Remember that tm_year is an offset from 1900, not the full year.
Remember that tm_mon ranges from 0 through 11.
localtime() and gmtime() may use shared static storage; copy the returned structure before another conversion call.
Check time(), localtime()/gmtime() and strftime() results before dereferencing or printing.
Use difftime() for differences between time_t values instead of assuming direct subtraction is portable.
Do not use calendar time as a monotonic performance clock; wall time may jump.

options: The number of days in the current year.
questions.explanation: tm_year is the number of years since 1900; add 1900 to obtain the calendar year.

questions.prompt: What is the valid month range for struct tm.tm_mon?
questions.explanation: tm_mon is zero-based, so January is 0 and December is 11.

questions.prompt: What does strftime return when the formatted result does not fit?
options: The required buffer size including the null terminator.
A pointer to the first character.
questions.explanation: A zero return indicates that no complete formatted string was written because the buffer was too small.

questions.prompt: Why should a program copy the struct tm returned by localtime before calling another time conversion routine?
options: The returned pointer may refer to shared static storage that a later call can overwrite.
The pointer always refers to dynamically allocated memory.
The structure is immutable and cannot be copied.
The function returns a pointer to the input time_t.
questions.answer: The returned pointer may refer to shared static storage that a later call can overwrite.
questions.explanation: The standard conversion functions may use shared static storage, so retaining the pointer across another call is unsafe.

questions.prompt: Which function is intended to compute the difference between two time_t values?
questions.explanation: difftime returns the elapsed difference as a double without requiring assumptions about the representation of time_t.
